title: Sugar Johnny the cornetist and his furniture swindles
summary: Sugar Johnny, a corner-walking cornetist, sold furniture on credit, was glad to leave for Chicago and died there.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well, he was here in town. All of us was here. See, all of us was working here. But of course I formed up. You see, this here, this fellow here, he was glad to go. Sugar Downer. Sugar Downer was glad to go. He, if I told him like today, he'd be glad to go since last night. Because he was in trouble. Well anyhow, let's explain about his trouble because he's dead now. I know he's out of his troubles now.
I never did know much about the figure Johnny.
He used to walk around the district every time you see a corner player missing. Johnny's dead in the district with his corner, walking around. Nobody was playing, nobody regular. You know?
Always looking for a job, hoping to get a job.

Always looking around, everybody says, the corner player never showed up. You see Johnny with his corner walking around, stopping in the halls and all around. Said, there's Johnny. Come on in there, Johnny. Johnny shoot the pieces, he know. You know? Was he a good corner player boy? Well he was pretty good. He was like Sam Bo. You know Sam Bo? Yeah. Sam Bo, this, somebody behind him is alright. You know? And if he knows something, he gonna shoot it. Big belly, he gonna shoot what he knows. But what he don't know, somebody else plays something, what he don't know, he just pull in. Yeah. And walk in like he knows. You know? Of course. Well, you know, a fellow, a good man in front of you, it's just like getting a good mule. And let the good mule, two good mules pull that old slow throw up, he gonna make us get up a little bit. Yeah. But the other fellow be pulling him. Well that's the same thing Sam Bo. And this other fellow, Eddie Morrison. Well, they tell me there's two fellows to make a good band between you and I. Nobody knows, but plenty of good musicians know them, you know? Yeah. But they talk, they got plenty of mouth, they can talk about how good they is, they play for the President and Roosevelt. And they ain't play nowhere. See? So finished that name, Johnny, he takes, he was glad to get away from you, quicker than he wanted to get away. Of course I didn't know him. And his daddy was a preacher, living right down the line between Robson and Durbin. That's the way he used to live.

You mentioned something about the trouble. I'm gonna give it to you, and give it to you for a minute too. He's glad he's out of his debts. He always say, there's one day they got to pay. Well, he or his daddy was a preacher, but he stayed, his daddy was staying there, but he stayed there. And he'd go somewhere else and move, then he'd go across the street and move, then he'd go down downtown and move. And every time you see him, he had a new set of furniture. But every time your furniture come in, it wouldn't be too long before that furniture's gone. He'd sold it to the other fellow. See? See? So you see? And then they'd always be looking for him, they always give a wrong name. His name was Sugar Johnny. His name was John Harris. Then the next time his name was Walter Jane. I'm glad he didn't give Lloyd Keppit, because that was a, you know, the coach said, no, me. But of course I'd have some trouble, you know? But he'd give any name what comes to his mind. Well, he'd go to, see he'd go to Kepp's, and he'd get a set of furniture. Bring it in. He'd say, no, I'd give him five, ten dollars, deposit, and bring it here. But he'd say, no. He'd get another fellow, he'd sell it. He'd sell it. He'd sell it. Get about 25, he'd pay five dollars to get it in. And after that, and then he'd move. See? When he moved, well, they didn't know where he's at. They don't see his bills coming, his bills coming, but nobody paying him. So they come see about it. Then he'd say, hey, I'm going to move somewhere else. Of course it wasn't strict like today, you know? Them days and time, it was, oh, he's deader than Connie. But then nobody would catch him. So when I look around again, he must have got about four or five sets of furniture. From, from, what do you say again? The border guards, cats, all of them smart people. But he outsmarted them. See? He outsmarted them. I don't know how smart them, but he outsmarted them out their furniture. And he never paid for it. See? He'd give the deposit to bring them. Then he'd go and sell it. Then, you know, what's the matter? And Chica John was glad when I told him, but you want to come, Johnny? I says, I've got a job to go away. You want to? Yeah, yeah. He was kind of a bracket face, you know? I says, well, we're going to leave. When? When are we going to leave? I said, well, we're going to leave next week. All right, Johnny. Duck and duck and duck, duck and duck and duck until the time come. Johnny. Then we had to go to rehearsal over the river at that photo theater. I don't know if you all heard about it. So we had to go over there. There's the head boss. There's the one getting the band together. Then they'll go sign a contract here with a lawyer. And when we get over there, sign another contract to bring us back. Well, that's two contractors agreements, you know? One to go and one to come back. Then I had to sign. So, all right. Well, Johnny duck and duck. I'll take it and brought it. When I brought him, Johnny takes in glad. He was the first one at the train. See? And Johnny said, all right. Well, I had the tickets. Johnny, the first one bought a train. The train hadn't coming yet. Johnny was there. And the first one on the train was Johnny. I didn't know what it was. Until way after that, I found out. Then Johnny, they were looking for Johnny for furniture business. And Johnny was in Chicago. And Johnny never had come back here. Johnny died over there. Died there. That's where he died.
